article_title: Early Risers
citation: Early Risers. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Children Classified as Having an Emotional Disturbance. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.med.umn.edu/psychiatry/research/earlyrisers/home.html
title: Four-component intervention model combining child skills, school support, parent skills, and family support
description: Early Risers organizes its intervention as four coordinated components. The Child Skills component teaches skills that enhance children's emotional and behavioral self-regulation, positive peer relationships, and academic success. The Child School Support component identifies areas of difficulty in the classroom and creates individualized plans addressed during normal school activities. The Parent Skills component is delivered in family night group sessions teaching positive parent-child relations, effective discipline, and school involvement, while the Family Support component uses home visits to identify basic needs and health concerns and implement plans for healthy lifestyles.
requirements: A family advocate coordinates the child- and family-focused components
Delivery across multiple years with both school-year and summer programming
target_learners: Elementary school children demonstrating early aggressive and disruptive behavior
target_learning_goals: Emotional and behavioral self-regulation
Positive peer relationships
Academic success
Effective parenting practices
examples: In August et al. (2003), the full-strength group received Child Skills components for two years plus the Family Support component, which included home-based therapy with a minimum of three bimonthly contacts in the first year and six contacts in the second year.
key_sources: Early Risers. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Children Classified as Having an Emotional Disturbance. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.med.umn.edu/psychiatry/research/earlyrisers/home.html

article_title: Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS)
citation: Faria et al. (2017). Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=early+warning+intervention+and+monitoring+system
title: Early warning monitoring cycle: identify at-risk students with attendance, behavior, and course performance indicators, intervene, and monitor progress
description: The pattern is a recurring school-level cycle in which a dedicated team uses routinely collected indicators — "engagement (attendance), behavior (suspension), and course performance (grades and credits)" — to flag students at risk of not graduating on time, assign them to interventions, and monitor their progress over time. The model is intended to help schools efficiently use data to both identify the at-risk population and provide targeted support.
requirements: A dedicated school team to lead and carry out the process
Data on attendance, suspensions, grades, and credits
target_learners: High school students in grades 9 and 10
target_learning_goals: Student persistence and progress in school
On-time graduation
examples: In the evaluation, EWIMS schools used the indicators to identify at-risk students and assign interventions, yielding lower chronic absenteeism than usual-practice schools.

article_title: Early Steps
citation: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Daily one-to-one tutoring session structure: re-reading, word study, sentence writing, new books
description: Early Steps sessions follow a repeating daily structure in which tutors use "a series of leveled, non-phonetic books" and "follow a daily schedule of re-reading familiar books, systematic word study, sentence writing, and introducing new books." This 30-minute, five-days-a-week structure recurs across the entire first grade year, giving each session a predictable sequence of familiar reading, word-level work, writing, and new text introduction.
requirements: One-to-one delivery in 30-minute sessions five days a week over the entire first grade year
trained tutors
target_learners: first-grade students
target_learning_goals: beginning reading skills including word attack and comprehension
examples: Tutors deliver the schedule daily across the first grade year in the evaluated urban Tennessee schools

article_title: The Preventable Failure
citation: Roderick, M., & Kelley-Kemple, T., with Johnson, D. W., & Ryan, S. (2021). The Preventable Failure: Improvements in High School Graduation Rates when High Schools Focus on the Ninth-Grade Year. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-preventable-failure
title: Use an early-warning indicator of ninth-grade course performance as the primary lever for dropout prevention rather than a packaged program
description: The report argues that effective dropout prevention should operationalize an early indicator of ninth-grade course performance and give school staff data tools to act on it, rather than purchase a packaged solution. CPS "placed the onus of the work in the hands of the principals," providing data tools that let educators identify at-risk students, monitor performance, and target recovery, while decentralized schools constructed their own approaches. The intervention supports staff to get ninth-graders to attend, complete homework, and get extra help when needed.
requirements: Requires giving principals access to real-time data linking attendance and course outcomes, plus clear evidence on the indicator's link to graduation
constraints: The article cautions the indicator is a very minimum standard of course performance, and that researchers could not isolate which component (data access, information, or principal commitment) contributed most
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in traditional urban high schools, particularly those at risk of course failure
target_learning_goals: Staying on-track to graduate through credit completion and passing core courses
examples: CPS included the Freshman OnTrack rate in its high school accountability system starting in 2007, and the Graduation Pathways office provided watch lists, monthly success reports, and credit recovery reports to schools
key_sources: Roderick, M., & Kelley-Kemple, T., with Johnson, D. W., & Ryan, S. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-preventable-failure

article_title: Teacher Career Paths, Teacher Quality, and Persistence in the Classroom: Are Public Schools Keeping Their Best?
citation: Dan Goldhaber, Betheny Gross, Daniel Player. (2011). Teacher Career Paths, Teacher Quality, and Persistence in the Classroom: Are Public Schools Keeping Their Best? Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, vol. 30, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Early-career teacher retention pattern: quality-graded sorting across the effectiveness distribution
description: The article describes a retention pattern in which the teachers who stay are, on average, the more effective ones: "more effective teachers remain in the profession and stay in their initial schools." At the same time, the pattern is not uniform, since "there appears to be heterogeneity in mobility behavior across the performance distribution," and mobility is also shaped by the student demographics and achievement levels of teachers' schools. The pattern therefore combines a positive average quality-retention gradient with context-dependent exceptions.
requirements: Teacher quality must be measured (here via value-added) to place teachers on the performance distribution
constraints: Pattern is documented for early-career public school teachers and is heterogeneous across the performance distribution
target_learners: early-career public school teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing teacher retention and quality
examples: The study tracks whether public schools keep their more effective early-career teachers, in the profession and in their initial schools

article_title: High School Graduation and College Readiness Indicator Systems
citation: Allensworth, E.M., Nagaoka, J., & Johnson, D.W. (2018). High school graduation and college readiness indicator systems: What we know, what we need to know. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://ncs.uchicago.edu/freshman-on-track-toolkit
title: Early warning and college readiness indicator systems: data organized into advance predictions of attainment to trigger strategic action
description: The report defines an indicator system as more than data: "At its most basic, an indicator provides a prediction of educational attainment (e.g., high school graduation, college graduation) well in advance of the outcome." Predictions are estimates that let practitioners change a student's trajectory, and only strategic use of information within data systems turns a piece of data into an indicator. The report distinguishes early warning indicators, which signal likelihood of high school graduation, from college readiness indicators, which signal likelihood of obtaining a college degree, and describes three uses: identifying students in need of intervention, focusing and assessing school improvement, and holding schools accountable.
requirements: A strong data system that produces setting-level and student-level indicators for schools to use in practice, which almost always requires district and state policymakers to provide resources for technology and personnel
Structures that provide guidance to educators around data use, since having data is not the same as having an indicator system
constraints: Predictions are not certainties; the report states that predicting an outcome is not the same thing as knowing that outcome will occur
The report omits description of system-level indicators, focusing on the school level consistent with the John W. Gardner Center framework
target_learners: High school students, particularly ninth-graders
Middle grades students
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College readiness and post-secondary enrollment, persistence, and graduation
examples: Chicago issues data reports generally every other week flagging ninth-grade students getting Ds or below in a core course or with low attendance
A student-level example is a list of ninth-graders updated weekly flagging students with low attendance or Ds/Fs; a setting-level example is first quarter attendance rates by period and subject
Figure 1 depicts policymakers, school support organizations, school leadership teams, and teacher and school staff teams all playing roles in effective indicator use

article_title: The effects of early college opportunities on English Learners
citation: Johnson, Angela, and Diana Mercado-Garcia. (2020). The Effects of Early College Opportunities on English Learners. (EdWorkingPaper: 20-232). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai20-232
title: Early College four-pronged theory of change for underrepresented students' postsecondary success
description: The article describes Early College as a dual-enrollment model whose design rests on a "four-pronged approach": whole-school enrollment, added academic and social supports, early exposure to college-level rigor, and credit accumulation. As the authors state, "EC aims to improve postsecondary success via a four-pronged approach: (1) it eliminates self-selection issues commonly experienced in dual-enrollment programs through whole-school enrollment" and three further aims covering supports, transition, and an academic head start. The study evaluates this model for English Learners.
requirements: Whole-school (cohort) enrollment in college courses through district-college collaboration
Structured advisories, tutoring, and informal academic and college counseling and mentoring
constraints: The study's findings suggest the model's effects may only partially extend to EL students, at least regarding immediate and four-year college enrollment
target_learners: English Learners in high school
Low-income, first-generation, and racial/ethnic minority students
target_learning_goals: College credit accumulation
High school graduation
Postsecondary transition and enrollment
examples: In the studied district, all 12th graders at three treated schools were registered by default and bused to a nearby community college, taking college courses in pathways such as media production, computer and information systems, and child development.
key_sources: Johnson, Angela, and Diana Mercado-Garcia. (2020). The Effects of Early College Opportunities on English Learners. (EdWorkingPaper: 20-232). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai20-232

article_title: Stuck at Red: Persistent Early Literacy Gaps and Later State Test Performance
citation: Lemke, M., Soo Ping Chow, A., LeBeau, B., & Quesen, S. (2025). Stuck at red: Persistent early literacy gaps and later state test performance. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Identify and support students at literacy risk as early as possible, because trajectories become harder to change in later grades
description: The brief recommends early, targeted intervention in kindergarten and grade 1 because students below benchmark tend to stay below benchmark and persistence worsens in later grades. It states that "identifying and supporting students early can help create the conditions for improved MCAS performance" and that findings "point to the importance and benefit of helping students meet benchmark as early as possible".
requirements: Statewide or school-level screening assessment data to identify students as at risk early in grades K–3
constraints: The brief notes current supports and interventions have not yet fully achieved desired improvements in outcomes after 1 or 2 years
Performance pathways to MCAS may not directly align with screening benchmark performance because the assessments measure different skills

target_learning_goals: Foundational reading and language skills
examples: The brief tracked students identified at significant risk across grades and found 64% of kindergartners versus 80% of grade 1 students remained significantly below benchmark a year later

article_title: From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration
citation: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/263
title: East Alabama Regional Cybersecurity Alliance (EARCA)
description: EARCA is a regional alliance established through collaborative efforts in Alabama Workforce Region 2 that aims to "expand economic opportunity in rural areas by bolstering the cybersecurity workforce ecosystem across multiple rural districts". It spans seven school districts (Anniston City, Etowah County, Oxford City, St. Clair County, Sylacauga City, Talladega City, and Talladega County), with more than 35,000 students positioned to engage, over half (52.5%) qualifying for free or reduced-price lunch. During SY 2024-25 it laid groundwork across partners, teachers, curricula (Project Lead the Way, TestOut, Code.org, plus IBM SkillsBuild), and student outreach, with each district launching at least one cybersecurity course in 2025-26.

career awareness and work-based learning in cybersecurity

article_title: Early Indicators and Academic Mindsets in the Clark County School District
citation: Snipes, J., & Tran, L. (2016). Early indicators and academic mindsets in the Clark County School District. San Francisco, CA: REL West @ WestEd. http://relwest.wested.org/
title: Districts implementing early warning systems should consider composite indicators and weigh the true-positive/false-positive tradeoff
description: The report recommends that districts using early warning systems focus on composite indicators combining attendance, credits, Fs, and GPA, because simple composites identified more than three quarters of eventual off-track students before high school entry. It also advises that "districts might consider trying to minimize false-positives in order to conserve resources" or, alternatively, "erring on the side of casting a broader net," since flagged students may still face elevated academic risk.
requirements: Student records data on attendance, credits earned, GPA, and semester Fs must be available for 8th graders before they enter high school.
constraints: Every indicator generated false-positives; the report states the results "consistently show a tradeoff" between correct identification and false-positive rates, and the choice among indicators is a policy decision about costs and benefits.
target_learners: 8th grade students transitioning to 9th grade in large urban districts
target_learning_goals: Staying on track for on-time high school graduation
examples: CCSD could share early risk indicators with high schools so supports could begin before or at the start of 9th grade; table 2 estimates per-school identified students, true-positives, and false-positives for each indicator.

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Early warning system methodology applied to school-level indicators of distress
description: The report proposes adapting early warning system methodology — commonly used to identify students at risk of not completing high school — to school-level indicators. An early warning system is defined as 'a process for identifying patterns and characteristics from previous events that turned out to be risky, testing those patterns in a local context to identify specific indicators and thresholds for risk, and then using the characteristics in a systemic way to identify scenarios of risk and to efficiently target interventions.' This report is presented as only a first step toward such a system for schools in distress.
requirements: Local validation: a historical reflection on characteristics of struggling schools must be done in each context to ensure identified data are those most likely to predict further struggling schools
constraints: The report does not itself build or validate thresholds; future publications are planned to support building context-tailored systems
target_learners: Charter school authorizers, charter support organizations, CMOs, and school boards
target_learning_goals: Identifying schools in distress before negative impacts on students are too severe to reverse
examples: The report suggests employing an early warning system may mean 'looking at existing data differently' in longitudinal fashion with an eye toward decline, rather than collecting vast reams of new data

article_title: Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming
citation: Menggian Wu. (2026). Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming. 2nd International Workshop on AI Literacy Education For All (ALIT4ALL 2026), co-located with AIED 2026, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
title: Seven-code labeling scheme for epistemic AI literacy indicators (inquiry relevance, aims, five strategies)
description: A construct-mapping scheme (Table 1) with seven binary analytic codes: inquiry relevance, mastery-oriented vs non-mastery-oriented aims, and five epistemic strategies (outsourcing, explanation-seeking, verification-seeking, prompt monitoring, epistemic justification). Each code carries a definition, regex-style lexical indicators, and example quotes, e.g., outsourcing as 'Delegating cognitive work without problem framing: pasting code/questions/errors with minimal interpretation or specific inquiry.' The scheme grounds both human annotation and automated LLM labeling.
requirements: Human expert annotation to iteratively develop and refine regex-based principles before automated labeling
constraints: Lexical indicators are probabilistic cues with a semantic gap, where context-sensitivity weakens the link between word usage and underlying intent
target_learners: undergraduate programming students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: observable epistemic engagement during AI-assisted problem solving
examples: Codes such as epistemic justification capture prompts questioning assumptions or asking for reasons and trade-offs, e.g., asking why y_test is used in a scoring method

article_title: Knowing Its Name, Not Its Nature: Word Association Mapping of Student AI Cognition and Evidence-Based Micro-Credential Design in Turkish Higher Education
citation: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00621-w
title: Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness (EAWR) micro-credential framework
description: The Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework is the study's proposed credential architecture, derived directly from the WAT diagnostic findings. The abstract states "the study proposes an Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework that bridges the gap between functional use and conceptual mastery". Unlike approaches that treat AI ethics as a separate add-on to technical curricula, the framework embeds ethical considerations throughout the competency structure. Each analytical layer of the WAT protocol generates a specific design implication for the framework, targeting the diagnosed absences: algorithmic transparency, ethical governance, and technical mechanisms that remain conceptually absent from students' associative networks.
requirements: A clear specification of the target competency domain grounded in empirical needs assessment, since the article states each effectiveness factor necessitates a clear specification of the target competency domain that extends beyond what normative frameworks alone can provide
constraints: The framework is proposed as a design output of this needs assessment; the article reports no implementation or outcome evaluation of the credential itself
target_learners: undergraduate students in Turkish higher education with high AI tool use but low formal AI education
target_learning_goals: AI literacy spanning functional use, algorithmic understanding, and ethical governance for workforce readiness
examples: The study uses the frequency, τ, MDS and network findings as a curriculum roadmap, positioning ethical content as foundational rather than an afterthought

article_title: Characterizing Students' LLM Usage Behaviors and Their Association with Learning in Critical Thinking Tasks
citation: Minju Park, Ivan Orozco Vasquez, and Cristina Conati. (2026). Characterizing Students' LLM Usage Behaviors and Their Association with Learning in Critical Thinking Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04534
title: Provide guidance on effective LLM usage early in the course, when usage differences most affect performance
description: The article recommends that instructors offer guidance on effective LLM use at the start of a course, because differences in how and how much students used LLMs were associated with performance gaps mainly on early assessments, with gaps narrowing as students gained experience. The authors state that "providing guidance on effective LLM usage early in the course may help accelerate appropriate and productive adoption."
requirements: Assessments must give students opportunities to experience the impact of their LLM usage on their own performance, or additional scaffolding, feedback, or explicit guidance may be necessary.

citation: Einziger Tzlil, Ben-Shachar Mattan S., Devor Tali, Shmueli Michael, Auerbach Judith G., Berger Andrea. (2021). "My Brain Can Stop": An ERP Study of Longitudinal Prediction of Inhibitory Control in Adolescence. Brain Sciences, 11(1), 100. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci11010100

constraints: The study tested prediction, not intervention: the design was not suitable to determine causal direction, and the sample was limited to males with a modest sample size and low rates of clinical-range symptom scores.
target_learners: adolescent boys at varying levels of familial risk for ADHD
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and inhibitory control
examples: The prospective longitudinal study measured paternal inattention at 2-6 months and child effortful control at 36 months, then showed these precursors directly predicted adolescent N2 amplitude at 17 years.

article_title: Measuring actual learning versus feeling of learning in response to being actively engaged in the classroom.
citation: Deslauriers L., McCarty L. S., Miller K., Callaghan K., Kestin G. (2019). Measuring actual learning versus feeling of learning in response to being actively engaged in the classroom. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1821936116
title: Instructors should intervene early in the semester to present the value of cognitive effort in active learning
description: The article recommends that instructors explicitly prepare students for the disfluency of active learning, because students initially mistake increased cognitive effort for poor learning. "We recommend that instructors intervene early on by explicitly presenting the value of increased cognitive efforts associated with active learning." Instructors should also give an assessment early so students can gauge actual learning, use research-based explanation and facilitation strategies, and solicit frequent feedback such as one-minute papers.
requirements: Instructors present evidence about fluency, feeling of learning, and actual learning early in the semester, and give an examination or other assessment as early as possible
constraints: Without this preparation, students can be misled by the inherent disfluency of active learning, which can negatively impact their actual learning during the first part of the course
target_learners: undergraduate students new to fully student-centered active learning, especially in large-enrollment college STEM courses
target_learning_goals: improved student motivation and engagement in active learning
accurate student self-assessment of learning
examples: A 20-min early-semester presentation describing active learning evidence and the negative correlation between feeling of learning and actual learning observed in this study; over 65% of students reported improved feelings about active learning by semester's end
